Sunlight looks white but contains all visible wavelengths, from long red waves to shorter blue and violet waves. When sunlight enters Earth’s atmosphere, it encounters molecules of nitrogen and oxygen that are much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light. This sets up a special kind of interaction called Rayleigh scattering, in which the light is redirected in many directions rather than simply passing straight through.

Rayleigh scattering is strongly wavelength-dependent: it scatters shorter wavelengths much more efficiently than longer ones, roughly in proportion to \(1/\lambda^4\). That means blue and violet light are scattered far more than red, orange, and yellow. As a result, when you look at a patch of sky away from the Sun, you are seeing sunlight that has been scattered toward your eyes by the atmosphere, and that scattered light is dominated by blue wavelengths.

Although violet is scattered even more than blue, the sky does not look violet for several reasons. The Sun emits less violet light than blue, some violet is absorbed in the upper atmosphere, and human eyes are more sensitive to blue than to violet. The brain combines these signals into the familiar blue sky. Near sunrise or sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere, so most blue light is scattered away before it reaches us, leaving the reds and oranges we see near the horizon.
